title: Reason: what God grants by prayer is not done by Saintly command—authors treat Saints as sub-God givers (Costerus)
source_text: LX. Certe ratio non patitur, ut quae precibus a Deo impetramus, ea dicamus facere jussu, potestate, praecepto. Ac proinde precum illarum authores aliud sibi voluisse videntur, quam ut simpliciter a Sanctis peterent, ut bona quae ipsos rogabant, precibus suis a Deo impetrarent; ac videntur Sanctos habuisse, non tantum pro suis apud Deum intercessoribus, sed etiam pro bonorum illorum, sub Deo, largitoribus, ac administratoribus; quales etiam Costerus, loco supra citato, testatur illos se existimare, asserens Sanctos esse administratores bonorum Dei. Unde postea concludit, Sanctos esse rogandos, tum ut pro nobis apud Deum intercedant, tum ut ipsi nobis opitulentur. Enchirid. cap. 12. in expositione quintae propositionis. Juxta quod idem Costerus scribens in hymnum, Ave Maris Stella, in verba istius hymni, solve vincla reis, hac utitur glossa, Solve precibus, solve meritis, solve authoritate, solve imperio. Externa omnia vincula solo nutu & voluntate removere potes. Et alia ejusdem hymni verba Mala nostra pelle, explicans: Mala igitur, inquit, nostra pelle oratione, meritis, potestate.
pass_a_gloss: Certainly reason does not allow that what we obtain by prayers from God we should say is done by command, power, precept. And therefore the authors of those prayers seem to have meant something other than simply asking of the Saints that by their prayers they obtain from God the goods for which they were asked; and they seem to have held the Saints not only as their intercessors before God, but also as bestowers and administrators of those goods under God; of which sort Costerus also, in the place cited above, testifies that they think themselves, asserting that the Saints are administrators of the goods of God. Whence afterward he concludes that the Saints are to be asked both that they intercede for us before God and that they themselves help us. Enchiridion chapter 12 in the exposition of the fifth proposition. According to which the same Costerus, writing on the hymn Ave Maris Stella, on the words of that hymn ‘loose the chains of the guilty,’ uses this gloss: Loose by prayers, loose by merits, loose by authority, loose by empire. Thou canst remove all external chains by nod and will alone. And explaining other words of the same hymn ‘Drive out our evils’: Drive out our evils therefore, he says, by prayer, merits, power.
pass_b_english: Reason: God’s gifts answered by prayer are not done by a Saint’s command.
Hymn authors treat Saints as under-God givers and administrators—Costerus: ask them both to intercede and to help.
His Ave Maris Stella gloss: loose by prayers, merits, authority, empire.

lemmas.gloss: loose by authority, loose by empire
